pamphlet_excerpts: North American Venomous Snakes: There are two types of venomous snakes in the United States (p. 22).
Pit Viper Head Anatomy: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) have triangular heads with pit marks on both sides of the head (p. 22).
Coral Snake Color Bands: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red and yellow separated by bands of black (p. 22).
Neurotoxic and Hemotoxic Venoms: Coral snakes inject powerful venom that works on the victim's nervous system; pit-viper venom affects the circulatory system (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Coral Snake Markings: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red and yellow separated by bands of black (p. 22).
Step 2 - Distinguish Venom Body Effects: Coral snakes inject powerful venom that works on the victim's nervous system; pit-viper venom affects the circulatory system (p. 22).
Step 3 - Carry a Hiking Stick: A hiking stick does double duty when you walk through places where snakes might lurk (p. 22).
Step 4 - Probe Brush Ahead Slowly: Walk slowly and use the stick to poke amongst ones and brush ahead (p. 22).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Three miles into a steep backpacking trek, a Scout feels a warm, rubbing 'hot spot' on their heel before any skin has blistered. According to Backpacking Requirement 1, what should the crew do?
quiz_item.question: Three miles into a steep backpacking trek, a Scout feels a warm, rubbing 'hot spot' on their heel before any skin has blistered. According to Backpacking Requirement 1, what should the crew do?
options: A. Hike faster for the next five miles until reaching camp so the foot becomes numb to the friction.
B. Pour untreated stream water into the boot to cool the heel and tighten the bootlaces as hard as possible.
C. Cut a hole in the hiking sock over the heel and apply antibiotic ointment directly to the wet wool.
D. Stop immediately, remove the boot and sock to let the foot dry, and apply moleskin or adhesive athletic tape over the hot spot before a fluid blister forms.

pamphlet_excerpts: Factors Determining Pack Weight: How much your pack weighs depends on the length of the adventure you have planned, the amount of food and equipment you must carry, and your personal (p. 53).
Twenty Five Percent Rule: For comfort on the trail, a pack containing everything you need for a safe trek should tip the scale at no more than 25 percent of your body's weight (p. 53).
Safe Weight Reduction Strategies: If your pack weighs more, here are some tips for lightening your pack without compromising your health or safety (p. 53).
Pre-Trip Gear Shakedown Purpose: Do a shakedown before every trip to "shake out" everything you won't need (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Evaluate Total Pack Weight: If your pack weighs more, here are some tips for lightening your pack without compromising your health or safety (p. 53).
Step 2 - Conduct a Gear Shakedown: Do a shakedown before every trip to "shake out" everything you won't need (p. 53).
Step 3 - Divide Shared Crew Equipment: Divide group gear so that each person carries a fair share (p. 53).
Step 4 - Upgrade to Lighter Gear: Gradually replace your heavy equipment and clothing with lighter items (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Backcountry Trail Courtesy Habits: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Stowing Emergency Mobile Phones: If you carry a mobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Respecting Quiet and Solitude: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Encountering Pack Animals Safely: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Keep Trail Noise Low: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Step 2 - Communicate With Lead Rider: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
Step 3 - Step Downhill For Horses: The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).
Step 4 - Yield to Uphill Hikers: If you encounter other hikers or backpackers going uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).

Seeking Low Ground Shelter: If astorm catches you, find a cave or a low spot among the rocks (p. 26).
Minimizing Your Lightning Target: Avoid prominent outcroppings, overhangs, and flood zones. If you cannot find shelter, become the smallest target (p. 26).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Locate Low Terrain Shelter: If astorm catches you, find a cave or a low spot among the rocks (p. 26).
Step 2 - Crouch Into Smallest Target: Avoid prominent outcroppings, overhangs, and flood zones. If you cannot find shelter, become the smallest target (p. 26).
Step 3 - Avoid Lying Flat Outdoors: Do not lie flat on the ground, because lying flat makes you a bigger target than crouching (p. 26).
Step 4 - Minimize Ground Contact Area: The less of you that is touching the ground, the better (p. 26).

pamphlet_excerpts: Practicing Trail Visitor Courtesy: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Stowing Emergency Phones Away: If you carry a mobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Respect Neighboring Campsite Quiet: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Three miles into a steep backpacking trek, a Scout feels a warm, rubbing 'hot spot' on their heel before any skin has blistered. According to Backpacking Requirement 1, what should the crew do?
options: A. Hike faster for the next five miles until reaching camp so the foot becomes numb to the friction.
B. Pour untreated stream water into the boot to cool the heel and tighten the bootlaces as hard as possible.
C. Cut a hole in the hiking sock over the heel and apply antibiotic ointment directly to the wet wool.
D. Stop immediately, remove the boot and sock to let the foot dry, and apply moleskin or adhesive athletic tape over the hot spot before a fluid blister forms.
choices: A. Hike faster for the next five miles until reaching camp so the foot becomes numb to the friction.
B. Pour untreated stream water into the boot to cool the heel and tighten the bootlaces as hard as possible.
C. Cut a hole in the hiking sock over the heel and apply antibiotic ointment directly to the wet wool.
D. Stop immediately, remove the boot and sock to let the foot dry, and apply moleskin or adhesive athletic tape over the hot spot before a fluid blister forms.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Stop immediately, remove the boot and sock to let the foot dry, and apply moleskin or adhesive athletic tape over the hot spot before a fluid blister forms.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Backpacking Requirement 1 stresses stopping at the first sign of a friction hot spot, drying the skin, and applying moleskin or tape immediately to prevent a debilitating blister.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. To let them know you are back safely so they do not report you missing or launch a rescue.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Upon your return, you must let your frontcountry contacts know you are back so they will not report you missing or initiate an unnecessary emergency response (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What should a backpacking crew do when encountering horseback riders or pack animals on a narrow trail?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What should a backpacking crew do when encountering horseback riders or pack animals on a narrow trail?
options: A. Hike quickly ahead until the trail widens into a clearing.
B. Climb onto high rocks on the uphill side of the trail so the horses can see you clearly.
C. Clap your hands to alert the animals of your presence before they get close.
D. Stop, ask the lead rider for instructions, and step a few paces downhill while standing quietly.
choices: A. Hike quickly ahead until the trail widens into a clearing.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Stop, ask the lead rider for instructions, and step a few paces downhill while standing quietly.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When meeting horses or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider, who will typically ask you to step a few paces downhill and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: If a lightning storm catches you in an open area without shelter, why should you crouch rather than lie flat on the ground?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: If a lightning storm catches you in an open area without shelter, why should you crouch rather than lie flat on the ground?
options: A. Lying flat makes you a bigger target for ground current, whereas crouching minimizes ground contact.
B. Crouching keeps your rain jacket from soaking through on wet soil.
C. Lying flat blocks your view of approaching thunderclouds.
D. Crouching allows you to hold onto metal trekking poles for balance.
choices: A. Lying flat makes you a bigger target for ground current, whereas crouching minimizes ground contact.
B. Crouching keeps your rain jacket from soaking through on wet soil.
C. Lying flat blocks your view of approaching thunderclouds.
D. Crouching allows you to hold onto metal trekking poles for balance.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Lying flat makes you a bigger target for ground current, whereas crouching minimizes ground contact.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Do not lie flat on the ground because lying flat makes you a bigger target than crouching; the less of your body touching the ground, the better (p. 26).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the practice of 'thumbnail navigation' during a backpacking trek?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the practice of 'thumbnail navigation' during a backpacking trek?
options: A. Measuring trail distances using the width of your thumb as a one-mile scale.
B. Keeping your map in your pocket and continuously matching surrounding terrain features to points on the map.
C. Pointing your thumb toward the sun to estimate cardinal directions without a compass.
D. Marking every campsite on the map margin with a thumbnail crease.
choices: A. Measuring trail distances using the width of your thumb as a one-mile scale.
B. Keeping your map in your pocket and continuously matching surrounding terrain features to points on the map.
C. Pointing your thumb toward the sun to estimate cardinal directions without a compass.
D. Marking every campsite on the map margin with a thumbnail crease.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Keeping your map in your pocket and continuously matching surrounding terrain features to points on the map.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Thumbnail navigation calls for constant awareness of your position by carrying your map in an accessible pocket and continuously matching terrain features around you with points on the map (p. 74).

options: A. Standard first-aid supplies do not work at high elevations.
